intro: Read the deck for the evidence and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide says what to remember, how to read the figures and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What the social determinants are
sections.big_idea: Most of what makes people ill happens outside the clinic, so **every sector's programme is a health programme** whether it says so or not.
in_plain_words: The social determinants of health are the circumstances in which people grow, live, work and age, plus the systems built to deal with illness. They explain why a child in the poorest fifth of Indian households is about three times as likely to die before five as one in the richest fifth.

Two ideas organise the rest of the course. Inequality is any measured gap, while inequity is a gap that is systematic, avoidable and unfair. And health follows a gradient: it improves at every step up the ladder, including steps far above the poverty line. **Measure inequality, argue inequity.**

diagram.caption: causes of the gap that no doctor alone can reach

key_terms.meaning: Circumstances in which people grow, live, work and age, and the systems for illness.
Any measured difference in health between groups.
A difference that is systematic, avoidable and therefore unfair.
Health improving at each step up the social ladder.
Target the poor because problems concentrate there.

worked_example.title: Inequality or inequity?
worked_example.setup: Three differences, sorted with the CSDH test of whether reasonable action could avoid them.
steps: Older people have more heart disease than younger people. This is biological and expected, so it is an inequality.
Only women die in childbirth. Also biological, so an inequality.
Under-five mortality is 59.0 in the lowest wealth quintile and 20.1 in the highest. The ratio is 59.0 ÷ 20.1 = 2.9.
That gap is systematic and avoidable by reasonable action, so a programme can call it an inequity and must explain why.
worked_example.answer: The first two are inequalities. The wealth gap of about three times is an inequity.

mistakes: Treating a health programme as separate from nutrition, sanitation or livelihoods work. Those programmes change health too.
Reporting 'inequity' without explaining why the gap is avoidable. It is a normative claim and carries a duty to explain.
Assuming that targeting the poor reaches the whole problem. Most excess deaths sit in the middle quintiles as well.
Mixing UN modelled estimates with SRS figures for India in one comparison.

recall.q: How did the WHO Commission describe the social determinants?
recall.a: The circumstances in which people grow, live, work and age, and the systems put in place to deal with illness.

recall.q: What is the difference between inequality and inequity?
recall.a: Inequality is any measured difference. Inequity is a systematic difference that is avoidable by reasonable action and therefore unfair.

recall.q: What did the Commission's 2008 report call for?
recall.a: Closing the gap in a generation.

recall.q: What did the 2025 World report say about the 2040 targets?
recall.a: Targets for reducing gaps in life expectancy and child and maternal mortality were likely to be missed.

recall.q: What does the gradient view add to the poverty view?
recall.a: Health improves at every step up the ladder, including steps far above poverty.

sections.title: Three frameworks: CSDH, Solar and Irwin, the rainbow
sections.big_idea: The CSDH chain explains **why** health is unequal and the rainbow shows **what** influences it, so choose the one that fits your question.
in_plain_words: Solar and Irwin's framework separates structural determinants from intermediary ones. Context and socioeconomic position sit first and decide who gets which conditions of daily life. Material, psychosocial, behavioural and health system factors act more directly on the body, and illness can feed back on a person's position.

Dahlgren and Whitehead's 1991 rainbow shows nested layers, from fixed factors at the core to general conditions outside. It is easy to explain to a panchayat. All three frameworks agree that most determinants lie outside health care, and they disagree on politics, targeting, behaviour and social capital. **Pick one framework per project.**

diagram.caption: the CSDH causal chain, from structure to outcome

key_terms.meaning: Context and socioeconomic position that sort people into hierarchies.
Material, psychosocial, behavioural and health system conditions.
A characteristic, such as income or caste, used to split a population.
A 1991 model of nested layers of influence.
Illness lowering a person's social position, for example through lost income.

worked_example.title: Place each factor on the chain
worked_example.setup: A farm labourer's family: no clean cooking fuel, mother with no schooling, TB in the household, loss of wages.
steps: The mother's schooling is a socioeconomic position, a structural stratifier.
Cooking with no clean fuel is a material circumstance, an intermediary determinant.
TB is the outcome on the chain.
Loss of wages from TB is the feedback arrow: illness lowers the family's position.
worked_example.answer: Schooling is position, fuel is intermediary, TB is the outcome, and lost wages are the feedback.

mistakes: Treating behaviour as pure choice. The framework places it as a channel because smoking and diet are distributed by social position.
Using the rainbow to explain why gradients arise. It says little about how layers produce them.
Forgetting the health system. The CSDH framework treats it as a determinant in itself.
Mixing framework vocabulary across a project's indicators and reports.

recall.q: What are the four boxes of the CSDH chain?
recall.a: Context, position, intermediary determinants and outcome.

recall.q: What does the rainbow answer?
recall.a: What influences health.

recall.q: What does the CSDH framework answer?
recall.a: Why health is unequally distributed.

recall.q: Name four intermediary channels.
recall.a: Material circumstances, psychosocial circumstances, behavioural and biological factors, and the health system.

recall.q: Which debate does Solar and Irwin flag about social capital?
recall.a: Depending on interpretation, it risks reinforcing depoliticised approaches.

sections.title: The social gradient
sections.big_idea: From Whitehall to NFHS, health improves at **every step** of the social ladder, so poverty alone cannot explain it.
in_plain_words: The Whitehall studies followed British civil servants, all in work, and found that the lowest grade had 3.6 times the coronary mortality of the highest. Smoking and other risk factors explained only part, and a second cohort found no narrowing over twenty years.

Three explanations compete: material, psychosocial and life course. In South Asia the material one carries more weight, and caste adds status assigned at birth. India's under-five mortality falls at every wealth step. **A gradient is a description**, and turning it into a causal claim needs further methods. Four traps can mislead you.

diagram.caption: each explanation implies a different policy

key_terms.meaning: Cohorts of London civil servants showing a mortality gradient by grade.
Money buys the conditions of health.
Low control and insecurity cause chronic stress.
Disadvantage in early life accumulates.
Universal action with intensity matched to disadvantage.
Illness lowering income or wealth.

worked_example.title: Steps on the wealth ladder
worked_example.setup: India, NFHS-5 under-five mortality per 1,000 by wealth quintile: 59.0, 48.0, 39.1, 32.7 and 20.1.
worked_example.answer: Every step is a fall, and the last step (12.6) is larger than the first (11.0).

mistakes: Reading a gradient as proof of cause without methods such as those in Impact Evaluation 101.
Ignoring reverse causation, where illness lowers wealth.
Quoting a flagged NFHS cell (in parentheses) without the warning.
Targeting 'below the poverty line' and assuming the rest are fine.

recall.q: What was the Whitehall I finding at 7.5 years?
recall.a: The lowest employment grade had 3.6 times the coronary heart disease mortality of the highest.

recall.q: What did Whitehall II find after twenty years?
recall.a: No diminution in the social class difference in morbidity.

recall.q: Name the three explanations for a gradient.
recall.a: Material, psychosocial and life course.

recall.q: What did the Marmot Review find after excluding the poorest and richest 5%?
recall.a: A 6-year gap in life expectancy remained.

recall.q: Name two ways to answer the traps of reading gradients.
recall.a: Use position measured before the outcome, show stratifiers jointly, standardise for age and region, or report intervals.

sections.title: South Asia: wealth, place and schooling
sections.big_idea: Wealth, place and mother's schooling each carry a gradient, and **the shape of the gradient** tells you what to do.
in_plain_words: NFHS-6 gives headline levels, such as stunting at 29.3%, but full breakdowns are not yet published, so the course uses NFHS-5 for gaps. Across India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan the poorest quintile does worse, though the shapes differ: a staircase in India, a flat top in Bangladesh and cliffs in Nepal and Pakistan.

Rural children do worse in every country, states differ more than eleven times, and urban averages hide slums. A mother's schooling predicts both mortality and stunting. **Match the policy to the shape**: a staircase calls for universal services with rising intensity, and a cliff calls for a targeted push at a specific barrier.

left.title: A staircase (India)
items: Every quintile better than the one below

right.title: A cliff (Nepal, Pakistan)
items: Jump or plateau at a threshold
A group cut off from facilities or roads
Targeted push can close much of the gap

diagram.caption: the shape of the gap suggests the policy

key_terms.meaning: A fifth of households ranked by assets and housing.
Height-for-age more than two standard deviations below the WHO median.
An area unfit for habitation under Section 3 of the 1956 Act.
Under-five mortality rate, deaths per 1,000 live births.
How IIPS describes the first NFHS-6 fact sheet.

worked_example.title: How big are the place gaps?
worked_example.setup: Under-five mortality per 1,000: India NFHS-5 rural 45.7, urban 31.5; Kerala 5.2, Uttar Pradesh 59.8; stunting lowest quintile 46.1%, highest 22.9%.
steps: Stunting ratio, lowest to highest quintile: 46.1 ÷ 22.9 = 2.0.
The state gap is by far the largest of the three.
worked_example.answer: Ratios of 1.45, 11.5 and 2.0, so state of birth separates children most.

mistakes: Comparing NFHS-5 and SRS levels in one chart. They measure different periods.
Quoting the urban average without noting that it hides slums.
Ignoring survey year. Pakistan's latest DHS in the API is 2017-18.
Using NFHS-6 for quintile or caste gaps before those tables exist.

recall.q: What is NFHS-6's national stunting figure?
recall.a: 29.3%, down from 35.5% in NFHS-5.

recall.q: Why do DHS breakdowns use ten years before the survey?
recall.a: To have enough births in each group.

recall.q: What did the 2011 Census count in slums?
recall.a: 6.5 crore people, 17.4% of the urban population.

recall.q: What does the mother's schooling table show for under-five mortality?
recall.a: 60.3 with no schooling falling to 24.9 with 12 or more years.

recall.q: What did IIPS estimate for life expectancy of the poor and non-poor?
recall.a: 65.2 and 69.0 years.

sections.title: Caste, tribe and gender
sections.big_idea: Caste, tribe and gender gaps **survive inside place and wealth**, and the direction of a gap must be checked, never assumed.
in_plain_words: Scheduled Tribe and Scheduled Caste children face under-five mortality of 50.3 and 48.9, against 32.8 for the Other group. The gap holds within rural and within urban areas, so place explains some of it and leaves most standing. Intersectional analysis shows women who are ST or SC, poor and rural carry the heaviest anaemia burden.

Gender acts before birth through sex selection and after birth through feeding and care. Spousal violence is socially patterned too. Religion offers a puzzle where the expected direction fails. **Collect identity data with purpose, consent and aggregation**, and prepare for the DPDP duties from 13 May 2027.

children.label: Caste and tribe
items: SC and ST children die younger
Steep for stunting, shallow for anaemia

children.label: Religion
items: Direction of gap is not predictable

diagram.caption: three stratifiers read in the same way

key_terms.meaning: Analysing class, caste and gender together instead of one at a time.
Sen's estimate of women absent from populations through sex selection.
Girls born per 1,000 boys.
Treating gender, class and caste as separate categories.
Only reporting groups large enough to protect individuals.

worked_example.title: Is the caste gap just a rural gap?
worked_example.setup: Under-five mortality NFHS-5, SC against Other: urban 39.0 and 26.3, rural 51.9 and 36.6; total ST 50.3 against Other 32.8.
steps: The ratio stays near 1.5 inside each place, so place is not the whole story.
worked_example.answer: Within each place the gap remains at about 1.4 to 1.5 times.

mistakes: Predicting the direction of a gap from other measures. Muslim under-five mortality is lower than Hindu in NFHS-5.
Using single-axis tables only. A group can be invisible in every one of them.
Collecting more identity data than needed, or storing it with names.
Treating a rising sex ratio at birth as the end of the problem.

recall.q: What is the ST under-five mortality in NFHS-5?
What spousal violence rate does NFHS-5 give for all women?
What was Sen's estimate in 1990?
recall.a: A great many more than 100 million women missing.

recall.q: What does the DPDP Act exemption s17(2)(b) cover?
recall.a: Processing necessary for research and statistical purposes, from 13 May 2027.

recall.q: What do ST and SC women share, per the IIPS intersectional analysis?
recall.a: A disproportionate burden of anaemia.

sections.title: Living conditions: water, sanitation, housing, air
sections.big_idea: Water, toilets, housing, fuel and air are shared conditions, and **four mechanisms** show where to intervene in each.
in_plain_words: Sanitation is a neighbourhood good: a child's risk depends on whether neighbours' faeces are contained. India's open defecation fell from 73% to 7%, yet administrative coverage and household surveys tell different stories, so use each for what it measures.

Housing, cooking fuel and air show the same pattern. Diderichsen's four mechanisms, exposure, vulnerability, consequences and feedback, give separate places to act. A drain cover cuts exposure, nutrition cuts vulnerability, insurance cuts consequences and schooling support interrupts feedback. **Name the mechanism each activity targets.**

key_terms.meaning: An improved facility not shared with other households.
Basic sanitation with excreta safely disposed of or treated.
WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, a modelled series.
Fuel that avoids indoor smoke from wood, dung or residue.
Indoor smoke from cooking fuel; its death rate fell 64.2% from 1990 to 2019.

worked_example.title: Who lacks clean cooking fuel?
worked_example.setup: NFHS-5 India: 58.6% of households use clean fuel overall, 89.7% urban and 43.2% rural.
steps: Women do most of the cooking, so the rural gap is a gap in women's exposure.

mistakes: Treating a declaration of open-defecation-free status as evidence of behaviour.
Counting toilets built as use. Check water, distance and whether every member uses it.
Reading an LPG connection as daily use. Households stack fuels.
Moving slum families far from work and measuring only the dwelling.

recall.q: What did JMP estimate for open defecation in India in 2019?
recall.a: 19.7% of the population.

recall.q: How many deaths did air pollution cause in India in 2019?
recall.a: 1.67 million, 17.8% of all deaths.

recall.q: Which housing criterion does PM-JAY use first?
recall.a: D1: households with only one room with kucha walls and kucha roof.

recall.q: What are Diderichsen's four mechanisms?
recall.a: Differential exposure, vulnerability, consequences and feedback to position.

recall.q: What is the lowest geography for NFHS sanitation indicators?
recall.a: District.

sections.title: Heat, food, roads, violence and work
sections.big_idea: Heat, food, roads and work show how **exposure and vulnerability follow position**, and why warnings and entitlements need practical routes.
in_plain_words: Heat risk follows work, housing and age, so Ahmedabad's plan cut the rate ratio for daily deaths at 47 degrees from 2.34 to 1.25. The National Food Security Act made grain a right, though grain addresses calories more than diet quality and anaemia stays high. Road crashes killed 1,68,491 people in India in 2022.

Work shapes health through hazard, security and protection. In 2025, 56.2% of workers were self-employed and 20.2% casual, so illness becomes lost income. Some occupations are now eligibility categories for health cover, which does not remove the hazard. **A warning helps only if the person can act on it.**

key_terms.meaning: A system that warns of extreme heat and triggers action across agencies.
National Food Security Act, 2013.
A household entitled to 5 kg of foodgrain per person per month.
2020 Act allowing schemes for gig and platform workers.
Urban eligibility by listed occupations.

worked_example.title: Grain for two households
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a priority household of 4 people and an Antyodaya Anna Yojana household, using the NFSA section 3(1) entitlements.
steps: AAY household: 35 kg per household per month, whatever its size.
Difference: 35 − 20 = 15 kg more for the AAY household.
Both are entitlements at subsidised prices, with a grievance mechanism in section 14.
worked_example.answer: 20 kg for the priority household and 35 kg for the AAY household, 15 kg more.

mistakes: Reading a heat message as protection when the person cannot stop work.
Reading the 1,190 deaths avoided as a precise effect. The interval is wide and the design is before-after.
Assuming grain coverage will fix anaemia.
Treating hospital cover as protection from workplace hazards.

recall.q: What entitlements does section 3(1) of the NFSA give a priority household?
recall.a: Five kilograms of foodgrain per person per month at subsidised prices.

recall.q: Who is head of household for ration cards under section 13?
recall.a: The eldest woman aged 18 or above.

recall.q: What share of Indian workers were in regular wage jobs in 2025?
What did Hess and colleagues estimate about deaths avoided each year?
recall.a: 1,190, with a wide interval of 162 to 2,218.

recall.q: What verb limits section 114 of the Code on Social Security?
recall.a: The Government 'may' frame schemes.

sections.title: Paying for health
sections.big_idea: How care is paid for is itself a determinant: **out-of-pocket spending impoverishes some families and shuts others out**.
in_plain_words: The chain runs from illness to cost, coping and lower position. India's out-of-pocket share of total health expenditure fell from 64.2% to 43.4%, with government's share rising from 28.6% to 43.7%. Read one year carefully, because 2021-22 was a pandemic dip.

Across South Asia the share runs from 79.3% in Bangladesh to 18.0% in Maldives. Catastrophic spending hides forgone care, a private stay can cost six to eight times a public one, and PM-JAY covers hospital bills but not outpatient costs. **Coverage on paper is a start**: use depends on awareness, documents and distance.

diagram.caption: how a health bill lowers a family's position

key_terms.meaning: Payments by households at the point of care.
National Health Accounts, India's tenth estimates for 2022-23.
Health spending above a share, such as 10%, of the household budget.
Ayushman Bharat scheme: Rs 5 lakh cashless hospital cover.
Needed treatment not sought because of cost.

worked_example.title: Changes in the financing mix
worked_example.setup: NHA 2013-14 to 2022-23: out-of-pocket share 64.2% to 43.4%; government share 28.6% to 43.7%; hospital stays Rs 4,290 public rural, Rs 27,347 private rural.
steps: Private insurance (3.4% to 9.2%) and social security (6% to 9.9%) also rose as shares.
worked_example.answer: Out-of-pocket fell 20.8 points, government rose 15.1, and a private rural stay cost 6.4 times a public one.

mistakes: Judging the trend from the pandemic year 2021-22.
Mixing denominators: NHA uses total health expenditure and WDI current health expenditure.
Reading a low catastrophic rate as protection when families forgo care.
Citing 2017-18 NSS costs without their date.

recall.q: What did the Commission say about catastrophic costs?
recall.a: Upwards of 100 million people are pushed into poverty each year.

recall.q: What was India's out-of-pocket share in 2022-23?
recall.a: 43.4% of total health expenditure.

recall.q: What did NFHS-6 find on household health scheme coverage?
recall.a: 60.2%, up from 41% in NFHS-5.

recall.q: When was PM-JAY launched?
recall.a: 23 September 2018.

recall.q: Name two costs PM-JAY leaves to other policies.
recall.a: Outpatient visits, medicines and tests outside a hospital stay, travel, food and lost wages.

sections.title: Policy approaches
sections.big_idea: Policy can be targeted, universal or **proportionate**, and the best design gives everyone a service with a dose matched to disadvantage.
in_plain_words: Health in All Policies asks non-health ministries to weigh health and equity before approving a road, scheme or lease. At district level it looks like a convergence committee with one shared outcome. Intersectoral action needs shared indicators, pooled budget and joint reviews, or each department reports only its own outputs.

Proportionate universalism, the Marmot Review's term, means universal action with scale and intensity proportionate to disadvantage. Pure targeting misses the middle of the gradient and risks exclusion errors. Health also appears in constitutions, and equity is a political choice as well as a technical one. **The design choice is itself a determinant.**

left.title: Poverty-line targeting
items: Misses the middle of the gradient
May lose support above the line

diagram.caption: two designs for the same programme

key_terms.meaning: Taking health and equity into account in every sector's decisions.
Departments agreeing shared indicators and joint reviews.
Universal action graded to the level of disadvantage.
A district body asking every department to report one outcome.
A check on who benefits, who pays and whether the gap changes.

worked_example.title: A ceiling on entitlement
worked_example.setup: Illustrative district: 200,000 rural and 100,000 urban residents. NFSA section 3(2) extends entitlements up to 75% of the rural and up to 50% of the urban population.
steps: The district has 300,000 residents, so at least 100,000 sit outside the entitlement.
worked_example.answer: At most 200,000 of 300,000 residents are entitled, so the ceiling leaves at least 100,000 outside.

mistakes: Assuming a health ministry can act on determinants alone.
Inverting the term to 'universal proportionalism'. The review's term is proportionate universalism.
Treating a targeting list as permanent. A list ages and creates exclusion errors.
Designing proportionate intensity without small-area data.

recall.q: When did the Helsinki conference on Health in All Policies take place?
recall.a: 10 to 14 June 2013.

recall.q: What does proportionate universalism require?
recall.a: Actions that are universal, with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage.

recall.q: Which constitutional article makes nutrition and public health a primary duty?
recall.a: Article 47.

recall.q: What did Paschim Banga hold?
recall.a: It is the constitutional obligation of the State to provide adequate medical services, and financial constraints cannot excuse it.

recall.q: What are the three questions of a health equity impact assessment?
recall.a: Who benefits, who bears the cost, and does the gap widen or narrow.

sections.title: Measuring inequity
sections.big_idea: Report gaps in **both** absolute and relative terms, use the whole distribution when you can, and keep the stratifiers in view.
in_plain_words: The rate ratio and rate difference compare two extreme groups. A gap can narrow on one measure and widen on the other, so say which you mean. The concentration index uses the whole distribution: rank everyone from poorest to richest and compare the cumulative health share with the population share.

PROGRESS-Plus keeps the stratifiers visible, and each data source offers a different set. Five errors create false equity stories: changed definitions, mixed sources, ignored sampling error, means only and relative change only. **Programme data rarely carry stratifiers**, so add two or three.

diagram.note: for grouped data; f is population share, h the rate, R the midpoint rank

key_terms.meaning: Outcome in the worse-off group divided by the better-off group.
Outcome in the worse-off group minus the better-off group.
Twice the area between the concentration curve and the line of equality.
Place, race, occupation, gender, religion, education, status, capital, plus extras.
The difference between two rates.
The ratio between two rates.

worked_example.title: Concentration index from quintiles
worked_example.setup: NFHS-5 under-five mortality by quintile: 59.0, 48.0, 39.1, 32.7, 20.1. Each quintile is 0.2 of the population, with midpoint ranks 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9.
worked_example.answer: C is about −0.19: deaths are concentrated among poorer children.

mistakes: Reporting only the ratio when the absolute gap is stuck.
Reading the grouped calculation as final. The slide says real analysis uses microdata with sampling weights.
Using programme data with no stratifiers and assuming reach matches need.
Comparing rounds with different indicator definitions.

recall.q: What is the rate ratio for under-five mortality, lowest against highest quintile?
What is the rate difference for the same pair?
What does a negative concentration index mean?
recall.a: The variable is concentrated among the poor.

recall.q: What does the 'Plus' in PROGRESS-Plus add?
recall.a: Personal characteristics associated with discrimination, features of relationships, and time-dependent relationships.

recall.q: Which source gives annual mortality but no wealth or caste breakdown?
recall.a: SRS.

sections.title: Practical application: an equity lens
sections.big_idea: Ten questions, matched stratifiers and the **shape of the gap** turn the course into a design review.
in_plain_words: The checklist asks which determinant a programme changes and for whom, how steep the gradient is, who could be excluded, and who owns the determinant. In delivery it asks whether reach matches need, whether costs to users are recorded, and whether gaps are tracked both ways.

Choose stratifiers by programme type, and keep categories identical to the national survey. Then read the baseline's shape: a steady gradient, a cliff, a high shallow gradient or a reverse gradient each calls for a different response. The three worked examples show allocation and monitoring. **A programme that cannot say who it is not reaching has not yet applied an equity lens.**

diagram.caption: match the response to the shape of the gap

key_terms.meaning: A review of a programme through stratified evidence.
Steady, cliff, shallow or reverse.
A written rule that survives staff turnover.
Ratio of rates or an absolute difference.
Comparing who is served with survey need.

worked_example.title: Reading the baseline for the ST poorest group
worked_example.setup: Illustrative block baseline: 1,200 children. Scheduled Tribe poorest two quintiles are 420 children, 48% stunted; OBC and Other are 30% stunted.
steps: Stunted children in the ST poorest group: 420 × 48 ÷ 100 = 201.6.
Absolute gap to OBC and Other: 48 − 30 = 18 percentage points.
worked_example.answer: About 202 children, an 18 point gap and a ratio of 1.6, so this group gets more intensity.

mistakes: Answering the checklist from memory without evidence. Where you cannot answer, record a gap.
Collecting too many identity questions, which adds burden and a data protection duty.
Allocating workers by headcount alone. A rule that is fair by headcount can widen a gap.
Reporting a fall in the average as success when the worst-off group is unchanged.

recall.q: How many questions are in the equity lens checklist?
recall.a: Ten.

recall.q: What does a cliff in the baseline suggest?
recall.a: An access barrier specific to that group.

recall.q: What should the endline report beyond the group changes?
recall.a: Change in absolute and relative gaps, and the concentration index if wealth was measured.

recall.q: Which stratifiers matter first for maternal and child health?
recall.a: Caste or tribe, mother's schooling, wealth and residence.

recall.q: What do you add for a comparison to attribute change?
recall.a: A comparison group, as in Impact Evaluation 101.

sections.title: Bringing it together
sections.big_idea: Ask of every programme which determinant it changes, for whom, and whether the gap closes, then **report the gap whichever way it moved**.
in_plain_words: The ten ideas split into concepts and evidence. Health is shaped where people grow, live, work and age. Inequity is avoidable and unfair, position works through intermediary conditions, and health runs along a gradient. On the evidence side: 2.9 times higher mortality in the poorest fifth, caste gaps inside every place, and 43.4% out-of-pocket.

The glossary fixes the vocabulary, and the related courses take each strand further: Public Health, then Inequality Basics, then the deck closest to your programme. Check the latest round before you reuse a figure. **NFHS-6 full tables, a new NSS round and the Census 2027 will change the numbers.**

key_terms.meaning: Health improving at each step up the social ladder.
Universal action graded to disadvantage.
Considering health and equity in every sector's decisions.
A -1 to +1 measure of wealth-related inequality.
Spending above a threshold share of household budget.
A checklist of stratifiers for equity analysis.

worked_example.title: Ask the closing question of a programme
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a sanitation programme baseline shows 55% of ST poorest households with no toilet used by all members, against 18% for OBC and Other.
steps: Which determinant? Sanitation, an intermediary material condition.
For whom? The ST poorest group.
Relative gap: 55 ÷ 18 = 3.1, so the gap is large on both measures.
worked_example.answer: Sanitation, for the ST poorest group, with a 37 point gap and a ratio of 3.1. The programme closes the gap only if both fall.

mistakes: Reusing figures from the course without checking the latest round.
Treating the glossary as optional, then mixing terms across indicators.
Skipping the order of study: Public Health, Inequality Basics, then the nearest deck.
Reporting only averages in a final report.

recall.q: What is the key sentence for any programme?
recall.a: Which determinant does it change, for whom, and does the gap close?

recall.q: Name two of the five evidence points in the summary.
recall.a: Under-five mortality 2.9 times higher in the poorest fifth, caste gaps survive within place, or households paid 43.4% of health spending.

recall.q: What does the concentration index measure?
recall.a: Twice the area between the concentration curve and the line of equality.

recall.q: What threshold does catastrophic spending use?
recall.a: 10% or 25% of household budget (SDG 3.8.2).

recall.q: What is the suggested learning order?
recall.a: Public Health, then Inequality Basics, then the deck closest to your programme.

notes.2: Treat the agenda as three movements. Sections 1 to 3 give you the ideas and frameworks, sections 4 to 8 give the South Asian evidence, and sections 9 to 11 turn it into policy, measurement and an equity lens. If you are short of time, read section 10 and then section 11.
notes.4: Start from the gap between the poorest and richest fifth of households: 59.0 against 20.1 deaths per 1,000 births. A better doctor alone will not close it, because the causes sit in water, fuel, schooling, debt and caste. **Any nutrition, sanitation or livelihoods programme is already a health programme.**
notes.5: Keep the two words apart. Inequality is any measured difference, some of it biological. Inequity is a difference that is systematic, avoidable and therefore unfair. Your rule of thumb: **measure inequality, argue inequity.** Your data show the first, and your reasoning about causes and remedies establishes the second.
notes.6: The Commission, chaired by Michael Marmot, reported in August 2008. Its sharpest claim is that health follows a social gradient in countries at every income level: the lower the position, the worse the health. It blamed poor policies, unfair economic arrangements and bad politics, so **the causes are made and can be changed**.
notes.7: Read the three recommendations as a ladder from daily living conditions, to the distribution of power and money, to measurement. Most programmes work on the first. Advocacy acts on the second, and **monitoring and evaluation teams contribute directly to the third**. Ask which rung your own work stands on.
notes.8: The 2025 report is the first global successor to the Commission, and its news is sobering: the 2040 targets for life expectancy and child and maternal mortality were likely to be missed. Remember the four areas for action, because section 9 uses them to frame what a South Asian programme can do.
notes.9: Compare the two views using the five quintile figures: 59.0, 48.0, 39.1, 32.7 and 20.1. Health improves at every step, even above poverty. **Targeting the bottom fifth helps those worst off but misses most of the excess deaths**, which also sit in the middle quintiles.
notes.10: Use this table to see the spread between neighbours: Sri Lanka's under-five mortality of 5.9 against Pakistan's 56.0. The figures are modelled estimates for comparing countries. For India itself, use SRS, which gives 29 overall, **33 in rural areas and 20 in urban areas**. Do not mix the two sources in one comparison.
notes.12: Hold the chain in your head: context, then socioeconomic position, then intermediary determinants, then the outcome. Structural factors get causal priority, because they decide who gets which conditions of daily life. **Name which layer your intervention changes** before you design indicators.
notes.13: Treat the six points as a mapping checklist to complete before design: governance, macroeconomic policy, social policies, sector policies, culture and values, and epidemiological conditions. The right-hand column is this course's own Indian illustration. **Write one sentence per point for your district** and notice which you cannot answer.
notes.14: Six stratifiers are correlated but not interchangeable, so measure each in its own way. In South Asia the last is best read as caste, tribe and religion. The slide's example makes the point: **a Dalit household in the top wealth quintile still faces caste discrimination**, which is why analysts report several stratifiers side by side.
notes.15: Sort any exposure into one of four channels: material, psychosocial, behavioural and biological, or the health system. Notice that the framework puts behaviour here because **who smokes and what people eat are distributed by social position**. Each row pairs the channel with an NFHS figure you can quote with its round.
notes.16: The framework treats the health system itself as a determinant, and it adds a feedback loop from illness to position. A farm labourer with TB loses wages. Because of this loop, part of the link between poverty and illness may run backwards, so **measure position before illness where you can**.
notes.17: The rainbow is a set of nested layers: fixed factors at the core, then lifestyle, networks, living and working conditions, and general conditions outside. The model was written to suggest quite distinct levels of intervention. Learn layer 3, the **living and working conditions**, because it maps onto government departments.
notes.18: Choose the model by the question you are asking. The rainbow answers what influences health and is easy to explain to a panchayat. The CSDH chain answers why health is unequally distributed and **suits a theory of change or evaluation design**. Use the rainbow to list departments and the chain to state your mechanism.
notes.19: Memorise the five agreements first, then the five debates. The debate on social capital deserves attention: a savings group helps its members but **leaves the public financing gap unchanged**. Pick one framework for a project, state it in the design document and use its terms consistently.
notes.21: Whitehall is the study that changed the question. All the civil servants had jobs and regular pay, yet the lowest grade had 3.6 times the coronary mortality of the highest at 7.5 years. Smoking, height and blood pressure explained only part, so **the gradient reached well beyond poverty**.
notes.22: Whitehall II asked whether the gap had narrowed in twenty years, and the authors found no reduction in the social class difference. Notice that even smoking is graded, falling from 33.6% to 8.3% across six grades. **Behaviour is distributed along the same ladder as the outcomes it affects.**
notes.23: Match each explanation to the policy it implies. Material explanations point to cash and services, psychosocial ones to job design and voice, and life course ones to early childhood. In South Asia the material route carries more weight, and **caste adds a fourth: status assigned at birth**.
notes.24: Read the bars as a staircase. Each quintile does better than the one below it, and the step from fourth to highest (32.7 to 20.1) is as large as the step from lowest to second (59.0 to 48.0). A 'below the poverty line' target **covers part of the first two bars and none of the rest**.
notes.25: England's version of the argument comes in three numbers: 7 years of life expectancy, 17 years of disability-free life, and a 6-year gap even after excluding the poorest and richest 5%. The third is the one to remember, because **removing both extremes still leaves a gradient**. Proportionate universalism is the review's answer.
notes.26: Use the traps and responses as a pairing exercise. Illness can lower wealth, wealth tracks caste and place, quintiles differ in age and region, and small groups carry wide intervals. NFHS parentheses flag thin cells, so **quoting a flagged figure without the warning overstates what is known**.
notes.28: NFHS-6 gives headline levels, and the slide labels each round. Read across: stunting fell from 35.5% to 29.3% and spousal violence from 29.2% to 22.3%. Notice that high blood sugar among women is higher in urban areas, so **not every gradient runs the same way**. Use NFHS-5 for group gaps until full tables arrive.
notes.29: All four countries show the poor doing worse, on different scales. These figures use ten years before the survey, so they differ slightly from five-year national rates. Pakistan's survey is from 2017-18, so compare it with care. **State the survey year beside every cross-country number.**
notes.30: Read the shape as well as the numbers. India is a smooth staircase, Bangladesh flattens at the top, Nepal jumps between second and middle, and Pakistan has two plateaus. A staircase suggests universal services with rising intensity, while **a cliff suggests a threshold, where a targeted push can close much of the gap**.
notes.31: Stunting in India is 46.1% in the lowest quintile and 22.9% in the highest, a ratio of about 2. The surprise is that nearly one child in four is stunted even in the richest fifth. That points to **shared determinants such as neighbourhood sanitation and mothers' height and nutrition**. Quintile data for NFHS-6 was not yet published.
notes.32: Rural children do worse in all five rows, and the urban figure is an average that hides slums. Two Indian sources give different levels because NFHS-5 covers the five years to 2019-21 and SRS measures 2023. **Never mix them in one comparison.** Nepal's rural gap (31 against 50) is wider than Bangladesh's (33 against 41).
notes.33: Kerala's 5.2 against Uttar Pradesh's 59.8 is a gap of more than eleven times inside one country. A child's state of birth carries differences in schooling, women's status, public services and political history. Solar and Irwin cite Kerala but note that the gains **have rarely been traced to the state's public policies**.
notes.34: The 2011 Census counted 6.5 crore people in slums, 17.4% of the urban population. The legal test for a slum, in the 1956 Act, is itself a list of determinants: unfit buildings, overcrowding, poor sanitation. **Disaggregate city averages by slum status**, and note that Scheduled Castes were 20.4% of slum residents.
notes.35: Read down the table: under-five mortality falls from 60.3 with no schooling to 24.9 with 12 or more years, and stunting from 46.3% to 25.7%. Schooling works through knowledge, a woman's say over money and food, and age at marriage. **Its effect is partly its own and partly a marker of the rest.**
notes.36: The IIPS estimate puts life expectancy at 65.2 years for the multidimensionally poor and 69.0 for the non-poor. A combined measure of education, health and living standards predicts longevity because it captures several determinants at once. Note the surprise: the gap was larger in urban areas (4.6 years) than rural (1.8).
notes.38: A Scheduled Tribe child faces 50.3 deaths per 1,000, about one and a half times the 32.8 of the Other group, with Scheduled Caste children at 48.9. The slide lists the routes: land and assets shaped by history, segregated settlements, discrimination in schools and clinics, and forest geography. **Give caste its own row in every table.**
notes.39: Use this table to answer the sceptic who says caste gaps are rural-urban gaps. Within urban areas SC children face 39.0 against 26.3 for Other, and within rural 51.9 against 36.6. **Place explains some of the caste gap and leaves most of it standing.** Cross-tabulations thin the cells fast.
notes.40: Two outcomes, two shapes. Stunting is steep by caste and wealth, while anaemia among women is high everywhere: even the richest fifth is at 51.0%. A shallow gradient on a high base argues for a universal programme with extra intensity, and **a steep gradient argues for directing effort down the ladder**.
notes.41: Single-axis tables can hide the worst-off group. The IIPS analysis looks at class, caste and gender together and finds ST and SC women carry a disproportionate burden of anaemia. So report combinations, for example rural ST women in the poorest two quintiles. **A group can be invisible in every single-axis table.**
notes.42: Sen's missing women argument rests on a ratio: 1.05 or 1.06 women per man in Europe, as low as 0.94 in South Asia. India's sex ratio at birth rose from 904 to 917 girls per 1,000 boys, which is welcome. **Gender acts before birth through sex selection and after birth through feeding and care.**
notes.43: Read the table as three gradients at once: spousal violence is 38.4% in the lowest wealth quintile against 16.9% in the highest, and 38.1% with no schooling against 17.7% with 12 years or more. The caveat is that one woman in six in the richest fifth reports it, so **design for universal access to help**.
notes.44: Do not guess the direction of a gap. Muslim children's under-five mortality (39.2) is lower than Hindu children's (42.8), although the two groups are spread almost evenly across wealth quintiles. The difference runs one way in rural areas and reverses slightly in urban. **Report religion and caste data so they cannot stigmatise a community.**
notes.45: Collect identity data with a purpose and with care: standard NFHS categories, an option to say 'prefer not to say', identity variables stored apart from names, and only aggregates reported. The DPDP duties in sections 3 to 17 apply only **from 13 May 2027**, so treat them as the standard to prepare for now.
notes.47: Climb the sanitation ladder from basic to safely managed. Bangladesh has almost eliminated open defecation at 0.0% yet only 37.3% have safely managed sanitation. A toilet that empties into an open drain still contaminates the neighbourhood. **Sanitation is a neighbourhood good**, which is why household wealth alone does not protect against it.
notes.48: The JMP series shows open defecation in India falling from 73% to 7%. The series is modelled, so it moves smoothly and began its fall well before 2014. The national figure hides where the rest is: rural India was still at 10.7% in 2024, in households **without space, water or money to maintain a toilet**.
notes.49: Keep two kinds of evidence apart. The administrative record says rural sanitation coverage rose from 39% to 100% by 2019, while JMP puts open defecation at 19.7% in 2019 and NFHS-5 found 19% of households with no facility. **Use administrative data for inputs and outputs and surveys for practice.**
notes.50: Housing works as both a health condition and an eligibility rule. PM-JAY's first rural criterion, D1, is a one-room household with kucha walls and roof. For your own baseline, collect rooms per person, roof and wall material, separate kitchen, water and sanitation. **Measure the determinants on both sides** when a programme relocates families.
notes.51: Four in ten households still cook without clean fuel: 43.2% of rural households use clean fuel against 89.7% of urban ones. Women do most of the cooking, so the rural-urban gap is **a gap in women's exposure**. An LPG connection is not daily use, so measure refills as well as ownership.
notes.52: The 1.67 million deaths were 17.8% of all deaths in India in 2019, with an economic loss of 1.36% of GDP. Ambient particulate deaths were 0.98 million and rising, while household air pollution deaths fell. **Exposure is shared but vulnerability is not**, since outdoor workers and people in poor housing bear more of the harm.
notes.53: Use Diderichsen's four mechanisms as a design tool: exposure, vulnerability, consequences and feedback to position. Each gives a separate place to intervene. A drain cover cuts exposure, nutrition cuts vulnerability, insurance and sick leave cut consequences. **Name the mechanism each activity targets** in your theory of change.
notes.54: Before choosing an indicator, check the lowest geography the source reaches. NFHS-5 gives district estimates across 707 districts, so a district team can compare itself with its state. The Census reaches villages and wards but is a decade old until the 2027 round is published. **A source you cannot disaggregate cannot target.**
notes.56: Ahmedabad's plan is a rare evaluated case. The rate ratio for daily deaths at 47 degrees Celsius fell from 2.34 to 1.25, with an estimated 1,190 deaths avoided each year. The interval is wide and a before-after design cannot rule out other changes, so **read the 1,190 as indicative**.
notes.57: Heat risk follows work, housing and age. The last vulnerability item carries the lesson: a daily-wage worker who stops at noon loses pay, so a warning is useful only if the work schedule can change. **Plans that shift hours and provide water act on exposure; plans that only send messages assume the person can act.**
notes.58: The Act turned subsidised grain from a scheme into a right with a grievance mechanism. Section 13 is a gender provision: the eldest woman is head of the household for the ration card, which changes who controls the entitlement. **Grain addresses calories more than diet quality**, so anaemia can stay high where coverage is wide.
notes.59: Two-thirds of children aged 6 to 59 months were anaemic in NFHS-5, and women's anaemia ranges only from 63.7% to 51.0% across wealth quintiles. When even the richest fifth has anaemia in half its women, **income alone cannot explain the pattern**. NFHS-6 does not yet report anaemia, so label the round.
notes.60: Roads are a determinant in two ways: they shape injury risk for pedestrians, cyclists and two-wheeler riders, and they shape access to care in labour or emergencies. The 1,68,491 deaths in 2022 came from police data, which undercounts injuries. **Pair crash records with hospital and survey data.**
notes.61: In 2025, 56.2% of workers were self-employed, 20.2% casual and 23.6% in regular jobs, so a health shock for most becomes an income shock. Note the verb in the Code on Social Security: the Government 'may' frame schemes. **The health effect depends on schemes being notified and funded.**
notes.62: Occupation now works as an eligibility category: PM-JAY uses 11 urban occupational categories, such as ragpickers, domestic workers and street vendors. The warning on the slide is that cover for hospital bills **does not remove the hazard**. Prevention sits with employers, contractors and the labour inspectorate.
notes.64: Follow the chain from illness to cost, coping and a lower position. The Commission called health care itself a determinant and said upwards of 100 million people a year are pushed into poverty by catastrophic costs. **Some families pay and are impoverished; others cannot pay and are missing from the spending statistics.**
notes.65: Read the three pairs together: out-of-pocket share fell from 64.2% to 43.4% while government's share rose from 28.6% to 43.7%. Even after that fall, households paid about 43 rupees of every 100 spent on health at the point of care. **Check both numerator and denominator when a share changes.**
notes.66: 2021-22 is a pandemic dip. Government raised spending to 1.84% of GDP as a one-time measure, and the out-of-pocket share fell to 39.4% before rising back to 43.4%. **A single pandemic year is the wrong baseline.** The slide's last line is the habit: when a ratio falls, check both parts.
notes.67: Compare Bangladesh at 79.3% with Maldives at 18.0%, and India at 43.9%. The denominators matter: this series uses current health expenditure, while India's NHA headline uses total health expenditure. The two are close for India but different. **Never mix denominators in one chart.**
notes.68: Catastrophic spending means more than a tenth of the household budget goes on health. India's 17.5% is from 2017, before PM-JAY's scale-up, so it cannot tell you the scheme's effect. The measure has a blind spot: **a household that forgoes care spends nothing and counts as protected**. Pair it with forgone care.
notes.69: Public and private care differ by a factor of six to eight: the totals are 4,290 and 4,837 in public hospitals against 27,347 and 38,822 in private. Even in public hospitals medicines and tests dominate. The NSS figures date from 2017-18 and predate PM-JAY's expansion, so **cite them with their date**.
notes.70: PM-JAY covers hospital care with Rs 5 lakh a year of cashless cover per eligible family, using SECC 2011 criteria such as D5 and D7 in rural areas. The slide's point is that **eligibility is built from social determinants**: housing, caste, household composition, landlessness and occupation. It is targeted, with a universal element for those 70 and above.
notes.71: Use the two columns as a gap analysis. PM-JAY addresses inpatient bills for listed procedures, and leaves outpatient costs, travel, wages lost, families without cards and places with no hospital nearby. NFHS coverage rose from 29% to 41% to 60.2%. **Coverage on paper is a start; use depends on awareness, documents and distance.**
notes.73: Health in All Policies asks non-health ministries to consider health and equity before approving a road, housing scheme or mining lease. It is hard because health is rarely the first goal of other ministries. At district level, picture **a convergence committee in which the Collector asks every department to report one shared outcome**, such as stunting.
notes.74: Convert the rainbow's middle layer into a list of departments, each with a shared indicator. Intersectoral action needs agreed indicators, pooled budget and joint reviews. **Without a shared indicator, each department reports its own outputs and nobody reports the outcome.**
notes.75: Proportionate universalism means universal service with a dose graded by disadvantage. The review warns that focusing solely on the most disadvantaged will not reduce the gradient. Picture it concretely: every child gets an anganwadi service, and **the worst-stunting blocks get more workers, home visits and food**.
notes.76: Compare four designs by strength and risk: targeted lists risk exclusion errors, broad entitlements with a ceiling cap coverage, universal-by-category schemes spend on some who could pay, and proportionate designs need good small-area data. **The design choice is itself a determinant**, because who is counted in shapes who gets care.
notes.77: Health appears in South Asian constitutions as a duty, a right and a judicial reading. Article 47 sets a primary duty, Article 21 was read in Paschim Banga to oblige hospitals to give timely treatment, and Nepal's Article 35 makes basic health services a right. **The case is about a poor man's access to emergency care.**
notes.78: Turn the Commission's third recommendation into routine practice: the same stratifiers in every round, gaps published beside averages, district estimates and a named office. The Census 2027 will include caste enumeration, giving denominators surveys cannot provide. **A health equity impact assessment asks who benefits, who bears the cost and whether the gap widens.**
notes.79: Equity is a political choice. Solar and Irwin cite research that the type of welfare state explained about 20% of differences in infant mortality among 18 wealthy countries. Use the table to turn the four areas of the 2025 report into programme actions, such as **avoiding digital-only access that excludes the poor**.
notes.81: Compute the two simple gaps from the same pair of numbers: 59.0 divided by 20.1 gives a ratio of 2.9, and 59.0 minus 20.1 gives a difference of 38.9 deaths per 1,000. The ratio tells you proportion and the difference tells you how many extra deaths. **Both use only the extremes and ignore the middle.**
notes.82: Absolute and relative gaps can disagree. In the NFHS table both narrowed, rural minus urban falling from 21.4 to 14.2 and the ratio from 1.62 to 1.45. The illustration on the slide shows them diverging, with the gap narrowing from 20 to 12 while the ratio widens from 2.0 to 2.5. **Always say which gap you mean.**
notes.83: The concentration index uses the whole distribution, ranking people from poorest to richest and comparing the health variable's cumulative share with the population's. It runs from -1 to +1, and a negative value means the variable is concentrated among the poor. **For an illness that is pro-rich inequality in health.**
notes.84: Work through the table in pencil. Multiply each quintile's rate by its share and midpoint rank, sum to 16.17, divide by the mean and subtract 1 to reach -0.19. The same method gives -0.14 for stunting, so **concentration is stronger for mortality**. The slide warns that real analysis uses microdata with sampling weights.
notes.85: PROGRESS-Plus is a memory aid for stratifiers: place, race and ethnicity, occupation, gender, religion, education, socioeconomic status and social capital. Walk through it for your own programme and note which letters your records lack. The Cochrane 'Plus' adds **personal characteristics associated with discrimination**, such as age and disability.
notes.86: Choose the source by the stratifier you need. NFHS and DHS give wealth, schooling, residence and caste, SRS gives annual mortality without wealth or caste, NSS gives spending, PLFS gives work and Census 2027 will give small-area denominators. **Add two or three stratifiers to your beneficiary records** to compare your reach with need.
notes.87: Check any equity story against five errors: changed definitions, mixed sources, ignored sampling error, means only, and relative change only. The NFHS-6 fact sheet itself warns readers to be cautious comparing trends because of smaller samples. **Read every first release with the same care.**
notes.89: Run the ten questions as a design review. Five are about design (determinant, worst-off groups, gradient shape, exclusion, other departments) and five about delivery (reach against need, user costs, two stratifiers, both gaps, feedback). **Where you cannot answer, record a gap to fill in the first year.**
notes.90: Match stratifiers to the programme: maternal and child health needs caste or tribe, mother's schooling, wealth and residence, while WASH needs residence, slum status and caste. **Keep categories identical to the national survey** so you can compare your beneficiaries with the population, and collect the minimum, since each question adds a data protection duty.
notes.91: Use the decision table by first diagnosing the shape of the gap. A steady gradient suggests a population-wide determinant, a cliff suggests an access barrier, a shallow gradient on a high base suggests a shared exposure, and a reverse gradient suggests diet or sedentary work. **Gap in use with equal need means fix the service.**
notes.92: Work the arithmetic yourself: the ST poorest group is at 48% stunted against 30% for OBC and Other, a gap of 18 points and a ratio of 1.6. Within ST households wealth matters too, 48% against 36%. **Neither caste nor wealth alone describes the problem**, and you must check each cell has enough children.
notes.93: Compare the two allocations of 30 workers. Option A follows headcount, while Option B gives every group a base level and adds intensity where the stunting gap is largest, moving 10.5 workers to 14 in the ST poorest group. **A rule that is fair by headcount can still widen a gap.**
notes.94: Read the plan as a template. Each indicator is stratified, paired with a gap measure and given a frequency. At endline report the change in each group and in both gaps. **A fall in the average with no change for the ST poorest is a result to report openly**, and attribution needs a comparison group.
notes.95: Scan the six mistakes against your last report. Averages hide the bottom, declarations are not outcomes, poverty-line targeting misses the middle, mixed sources distort, assumed directions mislead, and card numbers are not use. The closing line is the habit: **stratify, compare, ask why, and report the gap whichever way it moved**.
notes.97: Test yourself on the ten ideas by covering the right-hand column. The evidence side gives you anchor numbers: 2.9 times higher under-five mortality in the poorest fifth and 43.4% out-of-pocket share. Check the latest round before reusing any figure, since **NFHS-6 full tables, a new NSS round and the Census 2027 will change them**.
notes.98: Use the glossary to check you can say each term in one sentence. Pay attention to three pairs: structural and intermediary determinants, inequality and inequity, and proportionate universalism and plain targeting. **Define a term once in your design document and keep it fixed.**
notes.99: Follow the suggested order: Public Health, then Inequality Basics, then the deck closest to your programme. For heat and air, add Climate Essentials and Environmental Justice. For measurement, add Impact Evaluation and Survey Design. **Data Protection & the DPDP Act 101 matters before you collect identity data.**
